desc:
Cut the integer array arr into contiguous chunks, sort each chunk on its own, and concatenate the chunks in their original order. The values may be negative and may repeat. You want the concatenation to equal arr sorted in non-decreasing order.

Return the maximum number of chunks that makes this possible.

Example: arr = [2, 1, 3, 4, 4] returns 4: chunks [2, 1], [3], [4], [4].
hints: When is a cut between position i and i + 1 allowed? Think about the values on each side, not their positions.
After sorting each chunk, the glued array is sorted only if every element on the left of a cut is ≤ every element on the right of it.
That condition is: max of the prefix arr[0..i] ≤ min of the suffix arr[i+1..]. Precompute suffix minimums, sweep with a running prefix maximum, and count the allowed cuts; the answer is cuts + 1.
editorial: Consider a single cut. The chunks on the left are sorted among themselves and so are those on the right, so the final array is sorted if and only if no element on the left is greater than any element on the right at every cut simultaneously. For one cut between i and i + 1 that means max(arr[0..i]) ≤ min(arr[i+1..]). Equal values are fine on both sides, which is the key difference from the permutation version, where the test reduces to max == i.

Cuts are independent: if every individual cut passes the test, using all of them is valid, because each chunk then sits between neighbours that are no larger and no smaller than it should be. Using all allowed cuts gives the maximum, so the answer is the number of allowed cuts plus one.

Build sufMin from the right, then sweep from the left with a running maximum. Both passes are O(n); memory is O(n) for the suffix minimums. (A monotonic stack that keeps one maximum per chunk gives the same answer in one pass.)
